material.name: MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy
material.initial_state: random solid solution or chemically short-range-ordered state

intervention.description: Compare SRO and random-solid-solution atomistic samples

structure.description: BCC solid solution with or without local chemical short-range order

evidence_units.mechanism: SRO raises the double-kink formation cost for screw motion but enhances edge-dislocation mobility.

outcome.direction: edge mobility increases while screw double-kink nucleation decreases
outcome.measurement_method: molecular dynamics with machine-learning interatomic potential

comparison.direction: opposite effects for edge and screw dislocations

limitations: Atomistic simulation; effective mobility-model parameters represent distributed quantities.
evidence_spans: The mobility of edge dislocations is found to be enhanced by the presence of SRO, whereas the rate of double-kink nucleation in the motion of screw dislocations is reduced, although this influence of SRO appears to be attenuated at increasing temperature.
Independent of the presence of SRO, a cross-slip locking mechanism is observed for the motion of screws, which provides for extra strengthening for refractory high-entropy alloy system.

intervention.description: Compare SRO strengthening at 300 K and 2000 K

structure.description: SRO intersected by screw-dislocation double-kink formation

evidence_units.mechanism: The thermal entropy contribution lowers kink-pair formation free energy and weakens the additional SRO enthalpic barrier.

outcome.measurement_method: molecular dynamics fitted with a phenomenological mobility model

comparison.direction: SRO strengthening is diminished at 2000 K

limitations: The phenomenological fit treats distributed RHEA barriers as effective values.
evidence_spans: The strengthening effect due to SRO attenuates when temperature increases from 300 to 2000 K.
Based on the model, we can attribute this attenuation to the thermal entropy term
The strengthening induced by the presence of the local chemical SRO is found to be highly temperature-dependent; specifically, it is found to decrease at high homologous temperatures.
